2.solution: For hydrogen \(E_n = \dfrac{E_1}{n^2}\), so the third orbit has \(\dfrac{-E}{9}\) J.

3.subtopic: Ionic and Covalent Bonding, Lewis Structures and Octet Rule
3.solution: A \(\pi\) bond added to a \(\sigma\) bond pulls the atoms closer: C=C (134 pm) is shorter than C-C (154 pm). So (D) is false; the other three are true.

4.solution: Br has 7 valence electrons; three are used in bonds with F, and the remaining 4 form 2 lone pairs. So 2 lone pairs and 3 bond pairs (T-shaped molecule).

6.subtopic: First Law of Thermodynamics, Internal Energy and Work
6.solution: \(W = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -4 \times (10 - 25) = 60\ \mathrm{bar\,dm^3} = 6.0\) kJ done on the gas. For an ideal gas at constant temperature \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -W = -6.0\) kJ: 6.0 kJ of heat is released.

7.subtopic: Thermochemistry, Hess's Law and Bond Enthalpy

8.solution: Melting absorbs the enthalpy of fusion, so it is endothermic. Neutralisation, the Haber synthesis and freezing all release heat.

10.subtopic: pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water
10.solution: NaOH gives \(20 \times 0.1 = 2\) mmol of \(\mathrm{OH^-}\); \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) gives \(2 \times 10 \times 0.1 = 2\) mmol of \(\mathrm{H^+}\). They neutralise exactly, so the solution is neutral, pH 7.

13.solution: Fluorescein is an adsorption indicator. Before the end point the mixture is pale yellow (greenish-yellow fluorescein). Just past it, excess \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) on the AgCl surface adsorbs the fluoresceinate ion and the precipitate turns reddish pink.

14.subtopic: Group 1 Alkali Metals, Properties and Reactivity
14.solution: Small, highly polarising cations hold water strongly: LiCl crystallises as \(\mathrm{LiCl \cdot 2H_2O}\), magnesium chloride as \(\mathrm{MgCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O}\) and beryllium chloride as \(\mathrm{BeCl_2 \cdot 4H_2O}\). The large \(\mathrm{Cs^+}\) ion has a very low hydration enthalpy, so CsCl crystallises anhydrous.

15.subtopic: IUPAC Nomenclature, Functional Groups and Homologous Series
15.solution: \(\mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_2COOH}\) is butanoic acid. Removing one \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) gives propanoic acid (the first lower homologue); removing two gives ethanoic acid.

16.solution: The compound is \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CHI{-}CH(CH_3){-}CH(CH_3){-}CH(CH_3){-}CH_3}\). C-2 (H, I, \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), the rest of the chain), C-3 and C-4 each carry four different groups. C-5 carries two methyl groups, so it is not chiral. Three chiral carbons.

17.subtopic: Preparation Methods of Aldehydes and Ketones
17.solution: This is the Etard reaction: chromyl chloride forms a chromium complex A with toluene, and its hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde, B.

18.solution: Calcium carbide and water give acetylene: \(\mathrm{CaC_2 + 2H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_2 + Ca(OH)_2}\). A is ethyne.

19.solution: \(\rho a^3\) is the mass of one unit cell, and a bcc cell holds 2 atoms. So 1 g contains \(\dfrac{2}{6.6 \times 10^{-22}} = 3.03 \times 10^{21}\) atoms.

20.subtopic: Crystal Defects, Magnetic Properties and Semiconductors
20.solution: An n-type dopant has one more valence electron than Ge: phosphorus (group 15). B, In and Ga (group 13) give p-type.

21.solution: A bcc lattice is \(68\%\) packed, so \(32\%\) is void: \(0.32 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-23} = 2.56 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).

22.solution: For a dilute solution \(\dfrac{\Delta P}{P^0} = \dfrac{W_2 M_1}{M_2 W_1}\), so \(M_2 = \dfrac{6.4 \times 18}{0.016 \times 100} = 72\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\).

24.solution: An electrolyte gives more particles per formula unit (\(i > 1\)), and \(\pi = iCRT\), so its osmotic pressure is higher. A nonvolatile solute lowers the vapour pressure and raises the boiling point; it is the depression of freezing point, not the freezing point itself, that is colligative.

25.subtopic: Batteries, Primary, Secondary and Fuel Cells
25.solution: On discharge, at the positive electrode \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\) (Pb \(+4\)) is reduced to \(\mathrm{PbSO_4}\) (Pb \(+2\)): the oxidation number decreases by 2.

26.subtopic: Molar Conductivity, Kohlrausch's Law and Degree of Dissociation
26.solution: A straight line of \(\Lambda\) against \(\sqrt{c}\) with a finite intercept is the behaviour of a strong electrolyte. Sodium acetate is a salt (strong electrolyte); the other three are weak.

27.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
27.solution: \(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{\text{reduced}} - E^0_{\text{oxidised}}\). (A): \(-0.44 - 0.79 = -1.23\) V, negative, so it is non-spontaneous. (B) \(+2.00\) V, (C) \(+0.78\) V and (D) \(+1.22\) V are spontaneous.

30.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression
30.solution: The experimental rate law for \(\mathrm{2NO_2 + F_2}\) is \(r = k[\mathrm{NO_2}][\mathrm{F_2}]\), second order. Decomposition of \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) is first order, of acetaldehyde \(\tfrac{3}{2}\) order, and \(\mathrm{NO + H_2}\) third order.

31.subtopic: Group 18 Noble Gases and Xenon Compounds
31.solution: Xenon, with the lowest ionisation enthalpy of these, forms fluorides and oxides showing \(+2\), \(+4\), \(+6\) and \(+8\).

32.subtopic: Colour, Magnetic Properties and Spin-Only Formula

33.subtopic: Inner Transition Elements, Lanthanoids and Actinoids
33.solution: The actinoids end at lawrencium (Z = 103), so the first post-actinoid element is rutherfordium, Z = 104.

35.solution: In the spectrochemical series \(\mathrm{Br^- < OH^- < H_2O <}\) en, so bromide is the weakest-field ligand.

36.solution: Aqueous KOH supplies \(\mathrm{OH^-}\) as a nucleophile, so Cl is replaced by OH on the same carbon: butan-2-ol. (Alcoholic KOH would favour elimination to but-2-ene.)

37.subtopic: Preparation of Alkanes, Wurtz, Grignard and Decarboxylation
37.solution: Wurtz coupling joins two \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2C(CH_3)_2{-}}\) groups: \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}C(CH_3)_2{-}C(CH_3)_2{-}CH_2CH_3}\). The longest chain has six carbons with two methyls on each of C-3 and C-4: 3,3,4,4-tetramethylhexane.

38.subtopic: Physical Properties of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
38.solution: p-Nitrophenol forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds and packs well (m.p. about \(114\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)). o-Nitrophenol's hydrogen bond is intramolecular (m.p. about \(45\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\)); phenol and p-cresol melt near \(41\) and \(35\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

39.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Alcohols and Acidity
39.solution: Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + \(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\)) reacts through a carbocation; the tertiary carbocation forms fastest, so tert-butyl alcohol gives turbidity at once.

40.solution: Williamson's synthesis is an \(S_N2\) attack of an alkoxide on an alkyl halide. In bromobenzene the C-Br bond has partial double-bond character and the ring blocks back-side attack, so it does not react.
40.note: the printed structure in option B is written as a LaTeX formula; no figure needed

41.subtopic: Preparation Methods of Aldehydes and Ketones
41.solution: The Grignard reagent adds to the C\(\equiv\)N to give an imine salt X, \(\mathrm{(C_6H_5)_2C{=}NMgBr}\). Hydrolysis gives the ketone \(\mathrm{(C_6H_5)_2CO}\), benzophenone, with ammonia.

42.subtopic: Preparation Methods of Aldehydes and Ketones
42.solution: DIBAL-H (at low temperature) reduces an ester only as far as the aldehyde: \(\mathrm{RCOOR' \rightarrow RCHO + R'OH}\).
42.note: the printed reaction is written as a LaTeX formula; no figure needed

43.subtopic: Chemical Reactions and Basicity of Amines
43.solution: The carbylamine reaction needs a primary amine, and an aryl isocyanide needs an aromatic one: benzenamine (aniline) gives \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NC}\). The others are secondary or tertiary.

44.solution: In the Hofmann degradation \(\mathrm{RCONH_2 + Br_2 + 4KOH \rightarrow RNH_2 + K_2CO_3 + 2KBr + 2H_2O}\), the CO group is lost as carbonate, not reduced to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), so the amine has one carbon fewer. Reducing CO to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) is what \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) does.

45.solution: Citrus fruits are the classic source of vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

46.solution: Myosin (with actin) is the contractile protein of muscle. Keratin is in hair and nails, legumelin in legumes, and insulin is a hormone.

47.subtopic: Glycosidic Linkages in Di- and Polysaccharides
47.solution: Invertase (sucrase) hydrolyses sucrose to glucose and fructose. Maltase acts on maltose, trypsin on proteins, and amylose is a polysaccharide, not an enzyme.

48.solution: Polyacrylonitrile forms by chain addition across the C=C of acrylonitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCN}\). Nylon-6 (B), terylene (C) and PHBV (D) are condensation (ester or amide) polymers.
48.note: the printed structures in options A, C and D are written as LaTeX formulas; no figure needed

49.solution: Disposable cups and plates are usually moulded or foamed polystyrene.

50.solution: Viscose rayon is made in stages: cellulose is first treated with sodium hydroxide to give alkali cellulose, which then reacts with \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) to give sodium cellulose xanthate, and the xanthate is spun into acid. The first stage is cellulose with NaOH.

51.solution: \(\tan A + \tan B = \dfrac{4}{5}\) and \(\tan A\tan B = \dfrac{1}{5}\), so \(\tan(A + B) = \dfrac{4/5}{1 - 1/5} = 1\) and \(A + B = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

52.subtopic: Modulus and Argument — Polar Form, De Moivre and Square Roots
52.solution: By De Moivre's theorem the expression is \(e^{i14\theta} \div e^{i12\theta} = e^{i2\theta} = \cos 2\theta + i\sin 2\theta\).

53.subtopic: Counting Numbers and Geometric Figures — Digits, Divisibility, Points and Polygons
53.solution: There are \(2^5 = 32\) answer sequences; leaving out the one fully correct sequence gives at most 31 different students.

54.subtopic: Forms of a Line, Intersections and Concurrency
54.solution: The point is \((t, t)\) with \(t > 0\): \(t = 2t + c\), so \(c = -t < 0\). Of the options only \(-2\) is negative (the point is \((2, 2)\)).

55.subtopic: General Second-Degree Equation — Condition for a Pair, Parallel Lines and Distances
55.solution:
With \(h = 2\), \(b = -2\), \(g = 2\), \(f = 4\), \(c = 1\), the condition \(abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0\) gives \(-2a + 32 - 16a + 8 - 4 = 0\), so \(a = 2\).

The intersection satisfies \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}: 4x + 4y + 4 = 0\) and \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}: 4x - 4y + 8 = 0\), so \(x = -\dfrac{3}{2}\), \(y = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

56.subtopic: Two Circles — Touching, Common Tangents and Relative Position
56.solution: The second circle has centre \((-a, -2)\) and radius \(\sqrt{a^2 + 4 - 4} = |a|\). Touching internally: \(\sqrt{a^2 + 4} = 4 - |a|\), so \(a^2 + 4 = 16 - 8|a| + a^2\) and \(|a| = \dfrac{3}{2}\). Of the options, \(a = \dfrac{3}{2}\).

57.solution: The ellipse is \(\dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1\) and the line is \(y = -\dfrac{3}{4}x - \dfrac{k}{4}\). Tangency needs \(c^2 = a^2m^2 + b^2 = 16 \times \dfrac{9}{16} + 9 = 18\), so \(\dfrac{k}{4} = \pm 3\sqrt{2}\) and \(k = \pm 12\sqrt{2}\).

58.solution: \(S_1\) is true (\(n = 1\) gives 4). \(S_2\) is true (\(x = 1\)). \(S_4\) is true since every natural number is at least 1. \(S_3\) is false: \(x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0\) holds only for \(x = 2\) (and \(-5\)), not for every value. Only \(S_3\) is false.

59.subtopic: Logical Equivalence and Algebra of Statements
59.solution: \(\sim(a \to b) \equiv a \wedge \sim b\), applied twice: \(\sim[(p \wedge q) \to ((p \vee r) \to \sim q)] \equiv (p \wedge q) \wedge (p \vee r) \wedge q\). Since \(p \wedge q\) already makes \(p \vee r\) true, this is \(p \wedge q\).

60.solution: It has the form \((X \to Y) \vee (Y \to X) \equiv \sim X \vee Y \vee \sim Y \vee X\), which is always true. It is a tautology.

61.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
61.solution: \(\cot A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{4\Delta}\) and similarly for B and C. \(2\cot B = \cot A + \cot C\) gives \(2(a^2 + c^2 - b^2) = 2b^2\), so \(a^2 + c^2 = 2b^2\): \(a^2, b^2, c^2\) are in A.P.

62.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
62.solution:
Let \(t = \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\). \(|A| = 1 + t^2\) and \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{1 + t^2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & t \\ -t & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{B}{1 + t^2}\).

\(A^{-1}B = \dfrac{B^2}{1 + t^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 + t^2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 - t^2 & 2t \\ -2t & 1 - t^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\).

63.subtopic: Inverse of a Matrix — Adjoint Formula, Products and Verification
63.solution: \(2A + 3B = \mathrm{diag}(6 - 3,\ -10 + 6,\ 14 + 12) = \mathrm{diag}(3, -4, 26)\). The inverse of a diagonal matrix inverts each entry: \(\mathrm{diag}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, -\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{1}{26}\right)\).

64.solution:
\(\sin^{-1}(x - 2)\) needs \(1 \le x \le 3\) and \(\cos^{-1}x\) needs \(-1 \le x \le 1\), so \(x = 1\). Then the left side is \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 0 + \tan^{-1}3 + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{5} = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \tan^{-1}8\).

So \(\sec^{-1}\sqrt{k} = \tan^{-1}8\), giving \(\sqrt{k} = \sqrt{65}\), \(k = 65\). With \(\phi = \mathrm{cosec}^{-1}8\), \(\sin\phi = \dfrac{1}{8}\) and \(\cos 2\phi = 1 - \dfrac{2}{64} = \dfrac{31}{32}\).

65.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Principal Values and Evaluation

66.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Principal Values and Evaluation
66.solution: \(\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), whose principal \(\cos^{-1}\) is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). \(\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), whose principal \(\sin^{-1}\) is \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). The sum is \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

67.subtopic: Composite Functions — f∘g, Iteration and Functional Identities
67.solution: \(f(f(y)) = \dfrac{1 - \frac{1 - y}{1 + y}}{1 + \frac{1 - y}{1 + y}} = \dfrac{2y}{2} = y\), so f undoes itself and \(f(f(\cos x)) = \cos x\).

68.subtopic: Continuity at a Point — Finding f(c) and the Parameter
68.solution:
Numerator: \(4\sqrt{2} \cdot 2\sin 2x\cos x\). Denominator: \(\cos\dfrac{5x}{2} - \cos\dfrac{3x}{2} = -2\sin 2x\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\), so it is \(2\sin 2x\left(\sin\dfrac{3x}{2} - \sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right) = 4\sin 2x\cos x\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\).

So \(f(x) = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sin(x/2)}\) near \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), and the limit is \(\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{1/\sqrt{2}} = 4 = (2)^2\).

69.solution:
Multiplying repeatedly by \(2\sin x\): \(f(x) = \dfrac{\sin 32x}{32\sin x}\), so \(f'(x) = \dfrac{32\cos 32x\sin x - \sin 32x\cos x}{32\sin^2 x}\).

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(\sin 8\pi = 0\) and \(\cos 8\pi = 1\): \(f' = \dfrac{1}{\sin(\pi/4)} = \sqrt{2} = \mathrm{cosec}\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

71.subtopic: Derivative of One Function with Respect to Another
71.solution:
With \(x = \tan\theta\), \(\dfrac{\sec\theta - 1}{\tan\theta} = \tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), so \(u = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x\). And \(v = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = \sin^{-1}x\).

\(\dfrac{du}{dv} = \dfrac{1/(2(1 + x^2))}{1/\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}{2(1 + x^2)}\); at \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) this is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{5/2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\).

72.solution: \(y^2 = \cos x^2 + y\), so \(2yy' = -2x\sin x^2 + y'\) and \(y' = \dfrac{-2x\sin x^2}{2y - 1}\). Thus \(f(x) = -2x\sin x^2\), the derivative of \(\cos x^2\): \(\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx = \cos x^2 + c\).

73.solution:
The limit is \(\dfrac{f'(a)}{g'(a)}\). With \(x = \tan\theta\) and \(0 < x < \dfrac{1}{2}\): \(f = \cot^{-1}(\tan 3\theta) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 3\tan^{-1}x\) and \(g = 2\tan^{-1}x\).

\(f' = -\dfrac{3}{1 + x^2}\), \(g' = \dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}\), so the limit is \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\).

74.solution: The squared distance is \(x^2 + (y - 5)^2 = 4y + y^2 - 10y + 25 = (y - 3)^2 + 16\), least at \(y = 3\), \(x = \pm 2\sqrt{3}\). Of the options, \((-2\sqrt{3}, 3)\).

75.subtopic: Tangents, Normals, and the Slope of a Curve
75.solution:
\(x = \sqrt{9 - 3x^2}\) gives \(x = \dfrac{3}{2}\) (y is non-negative), so the point is \(\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)\). \(y' = \dfrac{-3x}{\sqrt{9 - 3x^2}} = -3\) there.

\(y - \dfrac{3}{2} = -3\left(x - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)\), that is \(3x + y - 6 = 0\).

76.subtopic: Tangents, Normals, and the Slope of a Curve
76.solution: \(2yy' = 3ax^2\); at \((2, 3)\) with slope 4: \(24 = 12a\), so \(a = 2\). The point lies on the curve: \(9 = 16 + b\), so \(b = -7\). Then \(7a - 2b = 14 + 14 = 28\).

77.subtopic: Trigonometric Integrals - Rational and Substitution Forms
77.solution:
\(\sin 4x = 4\sin x\cos x\cos 2x\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac{\cos x}{4\cos^2 x\cos 2x}\). With \(s = \sin x\): \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{ds}{4(1 - s^2)(1 - 2s^2)}\), and \(\dfrac{1}{(1 - s^2)(1 - 2s^2)} = \dfrac{-1}{1 - s^2} + \dfrac{2}{1 - 2s^2}\).

The integral is \(-\dfrac{1}{8}\log\left|\dfrac{1 + s}{1 - s}\right| + \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\log\left|\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{2}s}{1 - \sqrt{2}s}\right| + c\). So \(\alpha = -\dfrac{1}{8}\), \(\beta^2 = \dfrac{1}{32}\), and \(32(\alpha + \beta^2) = -4 + 1 = -3\).

78.solution: Put \(t = x^2\), \(dt = 2x\,dx\): the integral is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int t f(t)\,dt = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[t g(t) - \int g(t)\,dt\right]\) by parts, which is option (A) with \(t = x^2\).

79.solution:
\(\dfrac{3x + 7}{(x - 1)(x - 2)} = \dfrac{-10}{x - 1} + \dfrac{13}{x - 2}\), so the integral is \(-10\log(x - 1) + 13\log(x - 2) + c\).

Matching \(m\log(x - 2) - m\log(x - 1) + n\log(x - 2)\): \(m = 10\) and \(m + n = 13\).

80.solution: Put \(t = \sin^{-1}x\), \(dt = \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\): \(\displaystyle\int te^t\,dt = e^t(t - 1) + c = e^{\sin^{-1}x}(\sin^{-1}x - 1) + c\).

81.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
81.solution: \(\dfrac{1}{1 + \cos t} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\dfrac{t}{2}\), so \(f(x) = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}\) and \(f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}(1 + f^2)\). That is \(2\dfrac{df}{dx} = 1 + [f(x)]^2\).

82.subtopic: Odd and Even Integrands — Symmetric Limits
82.solution: \(\displaystyle\int_a^b x^3\,dx = \dfrac{b^4 - a^4}{4} = 0\) with \(a \neq b\) gives \(a = -b\). Then \(\displaystyle\int_{-b}^{b}(x^2 - x)\,dx = \dfrac{2b^3}{3} = 18\), so \(b = 3\), \(a = -3\) and \(a + b = 0\).

83.subtopic: Trigonometric Definite Integrals — tan x = t, Half-Angle Forms and Powers
83.solution: Put \(t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}\): \(5 + 4\cos x = \dfrac{9 + t^2}{1 + t^2}\) and \(dx = \dfrac{2\,dt}{1 + t^2}\). The integral is \(\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\dfrac{2\,dt}{9 + t^2} = \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

84.subtopic: Modulus and Greatest-Integer Integrands — Split the Interval
84.solution: On \([-1, 0)\), \(f(x) = x + 1\), and on \([0, 1)\), \(f(x) = x\). Each piece has area \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), so the integral is 1.

85.subtopic: Area Between Two Curves — Intersections First
85.solution: On \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\) \(\cos x \ge \sin x\): \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x - \sin x)\,dx = [\sin x + \cos x]_0^{\pi/4} = \sqrt{2} - 1\).

86.solution:
Treat x as the dependent variable: \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = -(x - e^{\sin y})\cos y\), that is \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} + x\cos y = e^{\sin y}\cos y\). The integrating factor is \(e^{\sin y}\).

\(xe^{\sin y} = \displaystyle\int e^{2\sin y}\cos y\,dy = \dfrac{e^{2\sin y}}{2} + c\).

87.solution: Put \(v = 9x + y + 5\): \(\dfrac{dv}{dx} = 9 + v^2\), so \(\displaystyle\int\dfrac{dv}{9 + v^2} = x + c\), that is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{v}{3} = x + c\), or \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9x + y + 5}{3}\right) = 3x + c\).

88.solution:
With \(\vec{n} = 2\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\): \(\vec{a} \times \vec{n} + \vec{b} \times \vec{n} = \vec{0}\), so \(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\) is parallel to \(\vec{n}\). Also \(|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^2 = 2|\vec{a}|^2 + 2|\vec{b}|^2 - |\vec{a} - \vec{b}|^2 = 6 + 18 - 16 = 8\).

So \(\vec{a} + \vec{b} = \pm\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\vec{n}\), and its dot product with \(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\) is \(\pm\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}(6 + 8 - 2) = \pm 8\sqrt{2}\). Then \(\sqrt{\lambda} = 8\sqrt{2}\) and \(\lambda = 128\).

92.subtopic: Foot of Perpendicular, Image, and Projection
92.solution:
A point of the line is \((-1 + 2t, 3 + 3t, -2 - t)\). The vector from \((2, -3, 1)\) to it, \((2t - 3, 3t + 6, -t - 3)\), must be perpendicular to \((2, 3, -1)\): \(14t + 15 = 0\), \(t = -\dfrac{15}{14}\).

The vector is then \(\dfrac{1}{14}(-72, 39, -27)\), parallel to \((-24, 13, -9)\). The line is \(\dfrac{x - 2}{-24} = \dfrac{y + 3}{13} = \dfrac{z - 1}{-9}\).

93.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
93.solution: The line is \(\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y - 2}{-1} = \dfrac{z - 3}{2}\), direction \((1, -1, 2)\); the normal is \((2, 1, 1)\). \(\sin\phi = \dfrac{|2 - 1 + 2|}{\sqrt{6}\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

94.solution: A point of the line is \((2 + t, -3 - 2t, -5 + 2t)\), at distance \(3|t|\) from \((2, -3, -5)\). So \(t = \pm 1\): the points \((3, -5, -3)\) with sum \(-5\) and \((1, -1, -7)\) with sum \(-7\). Of the options, \(-7\).
